title: When you're tired
hookLine: Dazhu's practice: when hungry, eat; when tired, sleep, and nothing added
tomorrow: so what made today good, and would you even notice?

lines: ONE MORE ITEM ON THE LIST.
DO YOU STILL MAKE AN EFFORT?
cards: It's the end of a long week, and a practice can turn into one more item on a list nobody can face. A Chan Buddhist teacher was asked about exactly this kind of effort.
A visiting master of the monastic rules asked Dazhu: do you still make an effort in your practice? Yes, said Dazhu. How?
When I'm hungry, I eat. When I'm tired, I sleep. The visitor wasn't impressed.

teach.b: Dazhu's answer: it isn't the same. When they eat, they don't just eat; they're full of a hundred demands. When they sleep, they don't just sleep; they're turning over a thousand schemes.
That's the Chan teaching, the school called Zen in Japan: practice is doing the one thing you're doing, wholly, with nothing added. Dazhu wasn't bragging about naps.
The visitor measured effort by how hard it looked; Dazhu measured it by whether anything extra came along. That's why it's harder than it sounds. The just is the whole practice.
And it's good news on a tired day, because the practice doesn't have to be long to be whole.
When the full sit is too much, this path keeps a one-breath version: one breath, breathed as just a breath, the same knowing breath from the rose-apple shade, only one of it.
Not a failed session. A whole one. Then sleep, and just sleep.

how: Chan and Zen students treat ordinary acts, eating and sleeping included, as practice when done wholly; people on this path keep a one-breath version for tired days.

o: a low day when the practice shrinks but stays
a medical sign you should see a doctor about
a reason to skip practice until next week

p: when hungry, eat; when tired, sleep

s: Dazhu said his practice was eating when hungry and sleeping when tired
and others, he said, don't just eat or just sleep; they add a hundred demands.
in Chan, practice only counts if it's long and hard
the popular idea. Dazhu's point is doing one thing wholly, nothing added.
the visitor agreed at once that Dazhu's practice was special
he objected that everyone eats and sleeps. Dazhu answered that they don't just eat or sleep.

games.q: a friend with a new baby says she's failed at meditation: she can't sit for long anymore. what fits Dazhu?
o: one whole breath, nothing added, is real practice; and when tired, rest wholly too.
she has failed: for Dazhu, the long daily sit is the only real practice.
she should wait until the baby is older; practice needs plenty of spare time.
games.why: Dazhu's practice was eating when hungry and sleeping when tired, wholly. a practice can be short and still whole.

practice: Let this whole sit be the tired-day version. Take one breath, in and out, and know it as just a breath, nothing added. Then rest, and if another breath comes, let it be just that one too.

wordCard.voice: When you're tired: the day the practice shrinks instead of stopping. Dazhu's way: when tired, sleep, and just sleep.

orig.note: Chinese: meditation, the name of Dazhu's school; Zen is its Japanese name.

carryVoice: Your line: one breath, with nothing added to it. Nine of fourteen, and now, rest.

sources.ref: Dazhu Huihai's exchange with a visiting Vinaya master ('when hungry I eat, when tired I sleep'; others 'make a hundred demands' and 'a thousand calculations'), Transmission of the Lamp (Jingde Chuandeng Lu), book 6
